dataflow.outcome: Stack memory overwrite with attacker-controlled bytes in process_message
dataflow.source: MQTT CONNECT packet client ID length and bytes
dataflow.summary: CONNECT body bytes -> cid_len -> memcpy into stack-local client_id[64]

impact.rationale: Attacker-controlled overwrite of a live stack frame can redirect control flow, leading to broker code execution or a crash.

likelihood.rationale: The overflow is a single packet with no protocol or authentication prerequisite.

preconditions: network reachability to the broker port
reachability.summary: Any unauthenticated TCP client that can reach the MQTT listener sends one CONNECT packet.

attackPath.summary: A remote client can corrupt the broker's stack before authenticating.

codeEvidence.explanation: cid_len comes directly from the packet (u16). memcpy copies cid_len bytes into the 64-byte client_id and index write client_id[cid_len] adds a NUL past the array when cid_len >= 64.
codeEvidence.label: Unbounded client ID copy into 64-byte field

codeEvidence.code: #define MQTT_CLIENT_ID_LEN                 64 // including nul char
codeEvidence.explanation: MQTT_CLIENT_ID_LEN is 64. Any client ID longer than 63 bytes overflows the destination.
codeEvidence.label: Client ID field is 64 bytes

codeEvidence.explanation: io_event io is allocated on the process_message stack. The connect union member and its client_id array are therefore on the stack, immediately before the saved frame state.
codeEvidence.label: Decoded packet is a stack local of process_message

confidence.rationale: The unchecked memcpy and the trailing NUL write are visible at mqtt.c:240-241; the destination is a 64-byte array in mqtt.h, and io_event is a stack local in process_message at server.c:860. Packet size is bounded only by max_request_size, so a multi-kilobyte client ID is accepted.

preventiveControls: Validate every attacker-supplied length against both the remaining packet size and the destination capacity before copying.
Keep decoded packet storage off the stack or use dynamically sized fields.
findings.remediation: Reject CONNECT when cid_len >= MQTT_CLIENT_ID_LEN or when cid_len exceeds the remaining packet body, and copy with a bounded length. Prefer allocating client IDs dynamically or enforcing the MQTT 3.1.1 23-byte minimum limit.
remediationTests: Send a CONNECT with a 64-byte client ID; assert it is rejected without corruption.
Send a CONNECT with a 4096-byte client ID; assert the broker rejects it and stays alive (ASan build).
Fuzz cid_len against lengths just under and over the 64-byte boundary.

rootCause.summary: The decoder trusts the packet-supplied client ID length and copies it into a fixed 64-byte array on the stack.

findings.summary: unpack_mqtt_connect reads an attacker-controlled 16-bit client ID length and copies that many bytes into connect.payload.client_id, a 64-byte array, then writes a NUL at client_id[cid_len]. The decoded packet lives in the stack-local io_event of process_message, so a CONNECT whose client ID exceeds 63 bytes overwrites the process_message stack frame with attacker bytes before any authentication.
findings.title: Pre-authenticated CONNECT client ID overflows a 64-byte field on the stack

validation.method: Static source review with attacker-controlled data-flow tracing
validation.summary: Source tracing shows a single unauthenticated CONNECT packet controls the copy length and the destination is the stack-resident io_event. No parser, size, or authentication check constrains cid_len before the copy.

dataflow.outcome: Heap overflow beyond a max_request_size allocation
dataflow.summary: PUBLISH with RETAIN -> retained_msg copy -> SUBSCRIBE -> memcpy(wbuf + towrite) and SUBACK append

impact.rationale: Heap corruption with attacker-influenced bytes can lead to code execution or broker crash.

likelihood.rationale: The sequence is simple and the default max_request_size leaves no headroom for the follow-up SUBACK.

preconditions: anonymous access enabled (default) or any authenticated session
retained flag set on the large publish
reachability.summary: Two unauthenticated connections suffice: one publishes a large retained message, another subscribes to the topic.

attackPath.summary: A remote publisher can place a large retained message and then cause another client to subscribe to its topic, overflowing the subscriber's heap write buffer.

codeEvidence.explanation: rbuf and wbuf are both try_calloc(conf->max_request_size, 1). No spare capacity or growth is reserved for responses.
codeEvidence.label: Write buffer is exactly max_request_size

codeEvidence.explanation: mqtt_pack writes the entire publish at wbuf + towrite, then towrite advances by len. Nothing checks towrite + len against max_request_size.
codeEvidence.label: Publish fan-out appends a whole packet to towrite

codeEvidence.explanation: Each retained message matching a SUBSCRIBE is memcpy'd at wbuf + towrite and towrite grows by the retained size.
codeEvidence.label: Retained-message replay memcpy has no capacity check

codeEvidence.explanation: The SUBACK is packed at the current towrite after all retained messages, so even a retained message that fills wbuf overflows by the SUBACK length.
codeEvidence.label: SUBACK is appended after retained replay

codeEvidence.explanation: towrite accumulates across queued replies and is reset only when the whole buffer has been sent, so consecutive outputs do not start from zero.
codeEvidence.label: towrite is only reset after a complete send

confidence.rationale: The allocation is exact at server.c:397-399. Appends at handlers.c:227-228 and 615-618 and 632-634, handlers.c:331-338, handlers.c:668-669 and server.c:338-339 add packet sizes to towrite with no remaining-space check. towrite is reset only after a complete send at server.c:652, so multiple queued outputs accumulate.

preventiveControls: Centralize all writes to wbuf in a helper that returns an error when the destination is full.
Size reply buffers from the actual packet being built and enforce a per-client output quota.
findings.remediation: Track the remaining capacity for wbuf and fail or disconnect when a reply would exceed it; grow the buffer dynamically for queued messages. Validate retained and fan-out message sizes against the destination's free space before packing.
remediationTests: Publish a retained message of size max_request_size - small, then subscribe from another connection under ASan; assert no overflow and either delivery or a clean rejection.
Queue two near-maximum publishes for one subscriber before its socket drains; assert the write path bounds the buffer.
Add a unit test that asserts every append checks towrite + len <= max_request_size.

rootCause.summary: Every response path treats the per-client write buffer as unbounded even though it is allocated with exactly max_request_size bytes.

findings.summary: client->wbuf is allocated with exactly max_request_size bytes, but SUBACK/UNSUBACK generation, retained-message replay, session resume replay and publish fan-out all append to wbuf + towrite without checking the remaining capacity. A retained PUBLISH close to max_request_size followed by a SUBSCRIBE (or two publishes delivered before the event loop flushes) writes past the allocation, corrupting heap metadata and adjacent objects.
findings.title: Unbounded writes into the fixed per-client write buffer corrupt the heap

validation.method: Static source review with attacker-controlled data-flow tracing
validation.summary: The fixed allocation and each unchecked append were traced. A retained PUBLISH of nearly max_request_size followed by a SUBSCRIBE reaches the retained replay memcpy and then appends a SUBACK past the end of wbuf.

dataflow.outcome: NULL or out-of-bounds function pointer dereference
dataflow.sink: indirect call through unpack_handlers[type] and handlers[type]
dataflow.summary: first MQTT byte -> type nibble -> unpack_handlers[type] / handlers[type]

impact.rationale: A single small packet terminates the shared broker process, disrupting every connected client.

likelihood.rationale: The triggering packets are trivially generated and no state or authentication is required.

reachability.summary: Any client able to connect to the broker port can send one two-byte packet.

attackPath.summary: An unauthenticated packet with an unimplemented type crashes the broker.

codeEvidence.code:
static mqtt_unpack_handler *unpack_handlers[11] = {NULL,
                                                   unpack_mqtt_connect,
                                                   NULL,
                                                   unpack_mqtt_publish,
                                                   unpack_mqtt_ack,
                                                   unpack_mqtt_ack,
                                                   unpack_mqtt_ack,
                                                   unpack_mqtt_ack,
                                                   unpack_mqtt_subscribe,
                                                   NULL,
                                                   unpack_mqtt_unsubscribe};
codeEvidence.explanation: unpack_handlers has 11 entries: index 0, 2 and 9 are NULL; indexes 11 and above are out of bounds. mqtt_unpack indexes it with the 4-bit packet type.
codeEvidence.label: Unpack table is shorter than the packet-type space and has NULL slots

codeEvidence.explanation: Only PINGREQ..DISCONNECT (12..14) return early. Every other type calls unpack_handlers[type], including NULL entries and types past the array end.
codeEvidence.label: Unchecked indirect call through the unpack table

codeEvidence.code:
static handler *handlers[15] = {NULL,
                                connect_handler,
                                NULL,
                                publish_handler,
                                puback_handler,
                                pubrec_handler,
                                pubrel_handler,
                                pubcomp_handler,
                                subscribe_handler,
                                NULL,
                                unsubscribe_handler,
                                NULL,
                                pingreq_handler,
                                NULL,
                                disconnect_handler};
codeEvidence.explanation: handlers[15] leaves index 0, 2, 9, 11 and 13 NULL; type 15 or greater would index past the array.
codeEvidence.label: Handler table also has NULL slots

codeEvidence.explanation: handle_command calls handlers[type] with the type derived from the packet header, without validating that the slot is non-NULL.
codeEvidence.label: Unchecked indirect call through the handler table

codeEvidence.explanation: The guard rejects only opcode < CONNECT or opcode > DISCONNECT, so CONNACK (2), SUBACK (9), 11 and 13 continue to the decoder.
codeEvidence.label: Opcode guard admits unimplemented types

confidence.rationale: unpack_handlers[11] has NULL at indexes 0, 2 and 9, while handlers[15] has NULL at 0, 2, 9, 11 and 13. server.c:512-513 admits opcodes 1 through 14, so 0x20, 0x90, 0xB0 and 0xD0 reach the unchecked calls at mqtt.c:434 and handlers.c:879.

preventiveControls: Guard both dispatch sites with a range check and a non-NULL check.
Use a single table sized 16 with explicit handlers for every defined type and reject the rest.
findings.remediation: Validate the packet type before both dispatch tables, reject every type the broker does not implement, and size the tables to the full 0-15 range with explicit NULL checks. Return a protocol error instead of calling through a missing entry.
remediationTests: Send 0x20 0x00, 0x90 0x00, 0xB0 0x00 and 0xD0 0x00 to a fresh connection; assert each is rejected with a protocol error and the broker remains alive.
Fuzz all 256 first bytes with a zero remaining length under ASan/UBSan.

rootCause.summary: The dispatch tables do not cover the entire packet-type space, and neither dispatch site validates table bounds or NULL entries.

findings.summary: mqtt_unpack indexes unpack_handlers[byte >> 4] and handle_command indexes handlers[type] without checking that the type is implemented. CONNACK (0x20), SUBACK (0x90) and the unmapped types 0xB0/0xD0 survive the opcode range check and reach a NULL function pointer or an out-of-bounds table read, crashing the single-process broker before authentication.
findings.title: Packet type dispatch tables contain NULL and out-of-bounds entries

validation.method: Static source review with attacker-controlled data-flow tracing
validation.summary: Table contents and both indirect calls were inspected. A two-byte packet with type 2, 9, 11 or 13 reaches a NULL or out-of-bounds function pointer before CONNECT, so no authentication is needed.

dataflow.outcome: Heap double free and allocator corruption
dataflow.sink: free_memory on the same tuples and topic strings twice
dataflow.summary: UNSUBSCRIBE packet -> unsubscribe_handler frees e->data -> process_message frees io.data again

impact.rationale: Double free corrupts the allocator and can be turned into controlled heap reuse, potentially code execution.

likelihood.rationale: Every UNSUBSCRIBE reply exercises the double free deterministically.

reachability.summary: A single pre-CONNECT UNSUBSCRIBE packet reaches the handler; CONNECT is not required.

attackPath.summary: One UNSUBSCRIBE packet frees the same heap objects twice.

codeEvidence.explanation: The handler frees e->data (which is io.data) and then returns REPLY.
codeEvidence.label: UNSUBSCRIBE handler destroys the decoded packet

codeEvidence.explanation: For REPLY, process_message calls mqtt_packet_destroy(&io.data) unless the type is PUBLISH. UNSUBSCRIBE is not exempt.
codeEvidence.label: process_message destroys the same packet for REPLY

codeEvidence.explanation: SUBSCRIBE and UNSUBSCRIBE share this case: every tuple topic and the tuple array are freed, leaving dangling pointers in the packet.
codeEvidence.label: Destructor frees tuple storage without clearing pointers

confidence.rationale: unsubscribe_handler destroys the packet at handlers.c:676. process_message destroys the same io.data at server.c:880. mqtt_packet_destroy frees pkt->subscribe.tuples and tuples[i].topic at mqtt.c:582-587 without nulling them.

preventiveControls: Define one owner for each decoded packet and document the ownership transfer at the handler boundary.
Null out freed pointers in mqtt_packet_destroy to make repeated destruction harmless.
findings.remediation: Remove the mqtt_packet_destroy call from unsubscribe_handler and let process_message own packet destruction, or transfer ownership explicitly. Make the destructor idempotent by clearing pointers and lengths after freeing.
remediationTests: Send UNSUBSCRIBE with one topic on a fresh connection under ASan; assert no double-free report.
Add a test that verifies process_message is the sole owner of decoded packet destruction.

rootCause.summary: Ownership of the decoded packet is split: the UNSUBSCRIBE handler frees it and the common dispatch loop frees it again.

findings.summary: unsubscribe_handler calls mqtt_packet_destroy(&e->data) before returning REPLY, and process_message then calls mqtt_packet_destroy(&io.data) again for every non-PUBLISH reply. The destructor frees the topic tuples without clearing the pointers, so a pre-CONNECT UNSUBSCRIBE triggers a double free of the tuple array and each topic string.
findings.title: UNSUBSCRIBE packet is destroyed twice, causing a heap double free

validation.method: Static source review with attacker-controlled data-flow tracing
validation.summary: Both free sites operate on the same io.data object and the destructor does not null the freed pointers. The UNSUBSCRIBE handler returns REPLY, which selects the second free in process_message.

dataflow.outcome: Out-of-bounds read, oversized allocation, or infinite loop terminating the process
dataflow.sink: try_alloc(len + 1) / memcpy(dest, buf, len) / try_realloc loop
dataflow.source: MQTT PUBLISH/SUBSCRIBE/UNSUBSCRIBE fixed and variable headers
dataflow.summary: remaining length and topic length are both attacker-controlled; usize subtraction wraps; unpack_bytes/realloc consume the wrapped size

impact.rationale: The underflow can crash or hang the shared broker and can expose memory through oversized reads.

likelihood.rationale: Crafting a truncated packet requires no special state and the wrapping arithmetic is unconditional.

reachability.summary: Any client can send a truncated PUBLISH/SUBSCRIBE/UNSUBSCRIBE packet; no CONNECT is required.

attackPath.summary: A short packet can force enormous allocation/copy sizes or an endless decode loop.

codeEvidence.explanation: len is usize. After subtracting 2 + topiclen, any packet shorter than the declared topic length wraps len to a very large value, which becomes payloadlen.
codeEvidence.label: PUBLISH subtracts topic length without a bounds check

codeEvidence.explanation: try_alloc(len + 1) and memcpy(dest, *buf, len) use the wrapped length. For SIZE_MAX the allocation size wraps and memcpy reads and writes far beyond the packet and the allocated chunk.
codeEvidence.label: unpack_bytes trusts the computed length

codeEvidence.explanation: When len is 1, len -= sizeof(u16) wraps to SIZE_MAX, so the loop does not terminate and repeatedly reads tuple headers past the received packet while reallocating.
codeEvidence.label: SUBSCRIBE loop subtracts without checking remaining bytes

codeEvidence.explanation: The same underflow allows an unbounded loop and out-of-bounds topic reads for UNSUBSCRIBE packets.
codeEvidence.label: UNSUBSCRIBE loop has the same unchecked subtraction

confidence.rationale: The subtraction sites are mqtt.c:314, 344/355/357 and 389/400. unpack_bytes at pack.c:411-417 uses the resulting len directly in try_alloc and memcpy. Because len is usize, any deficit becomes near SIZE_MAX rather than negative.

preventiveControls: Use checked subtraction helpers that return an error when the field does not fit in the remaining bytes.
Bound every decoder allocation by the received packet size.
findings.remediation: Before each subtraction, verify that the field length fits in the remaining bytes (remaining >= 1 + 2 + topic_len for SUBSCRIBE tuples, and remaining >= 2 + topic_len for PUBLISH). Reject truncated packets with a protocol error instead of subtracting.
remediationTests: Send PUBLISH packets with remaining lengths 0-4 and topic length 0 under ASan; assert a clean protocol error.
Send SUBSCRIBE and UNSUBSCRIBE packets with a single trailing byte; assert the decoder terminates with an error.
Fuzz remaining length, topic length and tuple count combinations under ASan/UBSan.

rootCause.summary: The decoder uses unsigned remaining-length arithmetic without validating each variable-length field against the bytes actually received.

findings.summary: unpack_mqtt_publish, unpack_mqtt_subscribe and unpack_mqtt_unsubscribe subtract header, topic and QoS lengths from the usize remaining length without checking that each field fits. A PUBLISH whose remaining length is smaller than 2 + topiclen wraps len to a huge value, and unpack_bytes then allocates len + 1 and memcpy's len bytes from the packet buffer. SUBSCRIBE/UNSUBSCRIBE loops similarly wrap and keep allocating and reading past the packet.
findings.title: Unsigned remaining-length arithmetic underflows in the MQTT decoder

validation.method: Static source review with attacker-controlled data-flow tracing
validation.summary: Each subtraction and the unpack_bytes sink were inspected. A three-byte PUBLISH with remaining length 1 and a zero topic length, or a SUBSCRIBE with one trailing byte, produces the underflow deterministically.

dataflow.outcome: Authentication bypass for PUBLISH; NULL session dereference for SUBSCRIBE/PUBACK/PUBREC/PUBCOMP
dataflow.source: any MQTT packet sent before a successful CONNECT
dataflow.summary: TCP packet before CONNECT -> process_message -> handle_command -> PUBLISH/SUBSCRIBE/ACK handler

impact.rationale: The broker's authentication boundary is bypassed for message injection, and premature session packets crash the service.

likelihood.rationale: No state or credentials are required; the first packet after connect can be PUBLISH or SUBSCRIBE.

preconditions: allow_anonymous=false to demonstrate the authorization bypass
reachability.summary: Any client can send PUBLISH or SUBSCRIBE as its first packet.

attackPath.summary: An unauthenticated client can publish into the broker and can crash it with premature session-dependent packets.

codeEvidence.explanation: process_message decodes and calls handle_command for the packet type. There is no client->connected or client->session test before dispatch.
codeEvidence.label: Every packet is dispatched without a connected/session check

codeEvidence.explanation: The allow_anonymous=false branch rejects missing or invalid credentials only while handling CONNECT. A PUBLISH never passes through this check.
codeEvidence.label: Authentication is only performed inside CONNECT

codeEvidence.explanation: subscribe_handler passes e->client->session to topic_add_subscriber and dereferences it via list_push; a pre-CONNECT client has session == NULL.
codeEvidence.label: SUBSCRIBE uses the session pointer without checking it

codeEvidence.explanation: puback_handler indexes c->session->i_msgs and c->session->i_acks with no check that c->session exists.
codeEvidence.label: PUBACK dereferences the session pointer

confidence.rationale: server.c:867 calls handle_command unconditionally. The allow_anonymous check is confined to connect_handler at handlers.c:366-375. subscribe_handler dereferences e->client->session at handlers.c:588/593, and the PUBACK/PUBREC/PUBCOMP handlers dereference c->session at handlers.c:793/817/847.

preventiveControls: Add an explicit connection state machine and authorize at dispatch time.
Treat any non-CONNECT packet received before CONNECT as a protocol violation and close the connection.
findings.remediation: Reject every packet other than CONNECT until the connection has completed a successful CONNECT and has a non-NULL session. Enforce authorization in the dispatch layer, not only in connect_handler, and return a protocol error for premature packets.
remediationTests: With allow_anonymous=false, send PUBLISH as the first packet and assert the broker rejects it and does not store a retained message.
Send SUBSCRIBE, PUBACK, PUBREC and PUBCOMP before CONNECT; assert each is rejected without a crash.
Add a state-machine test that only CONNECT is accepted in the initial state.

rootCause.summary: The packet dispatch layer has no connection-state authentication gate, so handler-level authentication in CONNECT can be bypassed and session-dependent handlers run with a NULL session.

findings.summary: process_message dispatches every decoded packet without checking client->connected or that a session exists. Authentication happens only inside connect_handler, so with allow_anonymous=false an unauthenticated client can still send PUBLISH (including RETAIN) and inject messages into broker topics. Session-dependent packets such as SUBSCRIBE, PUBACK, PUBREC and PUBCOMP similarly run with client->session == NULL and crash the broker.
findings.title: Packet handlers run before CONNECT, bypassing authentication and dereferencing a NULL session

validation.method: Static source review with attacker-controlled data-flow tracing
validation.summary: The dispatch call site and the CONNECT-only authentication branch were compared. PUBLISH has no session prerequisite and its handler performs no authorization, while SUBSCRIBE/PUBACK/PUBREC/PUBCOMP dereference the NULL pre-CONNECT session.

dataflow.source: attacker-chosen client ID and clean-session flag
dataflow.summary: client ID -> HASH_FIND_STR(server.sessions) -> shared session -> clean-session disconnect -> free while second client still references it

impact.rationale: A freed session remains reachable from a live connection, allowing heap reuse and potential code execution or data corruption.

likelihood.rationale: Client IDs are attacker-chosen and the broker never terminates the prior connection during takeover.

preconditions: two connections with the same client ID
reachability.summary: Two connections using the same client ID; the second uses clean_session=false and the first disconnects with clean_session=true.

attackPath.summary: An attacker can force two connections to share a session and then free it while the other connection continues to use it.

codeEvidence.explanation: When a session already exists and clean_session is false, cc->session is reused and session_present is set. The previous client remains connected and still points to the same session object.
codeEvidence.label: Existing session is reused without disconnecting the prior client

codeEvidence.code:
// Let's track client on the global map to be used on publish
    HASH_ADD_STR(server.clients_map, client_id, cc);
codeEvidence.explanation: HASH_ADD_STR inserts the new client under the same client_id key that the old client already uses, so lookups and deletions become ambiguous.
codeEvidence.label: A second clients_map entry is added for the same client ID

codeEvidence.explanation: client_deactivate frees client->session when the disconnecting client's clean_session is true, even if another connected client still references that same session.
codeEvidence.label: Disconnect frees the shared session

confidence.rationale: connect_handler finds cc->session by client ID at handlers.c:400 and keeps it when clean_session is false. It never closes the previous client, and it adds a second clients_map entry with the same key at handlers.c:425. client_deactivate frees the shared session at server.c:438-439 based only on the disconnecting client's clean_session flag.

preventiveControls: Implement MQTT 3.1.1 session takeover by closing the existing connection and removing its map entry before reusing the session.
Reference-count sessions by connection and free them only when the last owner releases them.
findings.remediation: On a duplicate client ID, disconnect and unregister the existing connection before adopting its session (MQTT takeover semantics), or reject the new connection. Keep exactly one clients_map entry per client ID and reference-count sessions by owning connection.
remediationTests: Open two connections with the same client ID and clean_session=false, then disconnect the first with clean_session=true and publish/subscribe from the second under ASan.
Assert the broker keeps exactly one clients_map entry per client ID after a takeover.
Add a takeover test that verifies the old connection is closed before the new connection adopts the session.

rootCause.summary: Session ownership is not exclusive to one connection: a reused session can be referenced by multiple clients and freed by whichever clean-session client disconnects first.

findings.summary: connect_handler looks up an existing session by client ID and reuses it for the new connection without disconnecting the old client or removing its clients_map entry. If the new connection keeps clean_session=false, both connections point at the same session; when the original connection later disconnects with clean_session=true, client_deactivate frees that session while the new connection still references it. Duplicate HASH_ADD_STR entries and the HASH_DEL of a shared session worsen the corruption.
findings.title: Duplicate client IDs share a session and free it while another connection still uses it

validation.method: Static source review with attacker-controlled data-flow tracing
validation.summary: The session lookup, the missing disconnect of the old client, the duplicate hash insertion and the session free on disconnect were traced as one ownership chain. Two connections with the same client ID are sufficient to obtain a dangling session pointer.

dataflow.outcome: NULL pointer dereference and broker crash
dataflow.summary: PUBREC pkt_id -> i_acks[pkt_id] set -> 20-second timer -> ACK branch -> mqtt_pack(NULL)

impact.rationale: The broker process terminates after a short delay, disrupting all clients, but exploitation is limited to denial of service.

likelihood.rationale: Requires a valid session and the retransmission interval, but the input is a single ordinary PUBREC.

reachability.attacker: network client with an MQTT session
reachability.summary: A connected (or pre-CONNECT PUBREC-crashing) client sends PUBREC with an unused packet ID and waits for the timer.

attackPath.summary: A connected client can make the broker dereference NULL during ACK retransmission.

codeEvidence.explanation: struct mqtt_packet *p = NULL is declared once for the whole timer callback; the message retransmission branch is the only assignment.
codeEvidence.label: p starts NULL and is set only in the message branch

codeEvidence.explanation: The ACK branch builds a local struct mqtt_packet ack but serializes p, which is NULL when no message was resent for this index.
codeEvidence.label: ACK branch passes p instead of &ack

codeEvidence.explanation: pubrec_handler writes c->session->i_acks[pkt_id] = time(NULL) without creating a corresponding i_msgs entry, so the ACK branch can run alone.
codeEvidence.label: PUBREC creates an ACK-only inflight entry

confidence.rationale: p is initialized to NULL at server.c:314 and assigned only inside the i_msgs branch. The ACK branch at server.c:354 calls mqtt_pack(p, ...) instead of mqtt_pack(&ack, ...). pubrec_handler sets c->session->i_acks[pkt_id] without creating an i_msgs entry.

preventiveControls: Serialize the packet that was built in the same branch and scope the retransmission pointer to each branch.
Validate packet identifiers before storing ACK state.
findings.remediation: Pass &ack to mqtt_pack in the ACK branch and compute the size from the same packet that is serialized. Reset p per iteration or avoid sharing it between the two branches.
remediationTests: Send PUBREC with an unused packet ID from a connected client, wait for the timer, and assert no crash.
Unit-test inflight_msg_check with an ACK-only session entry.

rootCause.summary: The retransmission helper reuses a pointer from the message branch for the ACK branch and never reinitializes it.

findings.summary: inflight_msg_check resends pending ACKs with mqtt_pack(p, c->wbuf + c->towrite), but p is only assigned in the preceding message branch and is NULL when only an ACK is pending. A client can create an ACK-only inflight entry by sending PUBREC for an unused packet ID; after the 20-second retransmission timer, mqtt_pack dereferences NULL and crashes the broker. The call also uses the wrong buffer size, since size was computed from the ACK packet.
findings.title: Inflight ACK retransmission packs through a NULL packet pointer

validation.method: Static source review with attacker-controlled data-flow tracing
validation.summary: The pointer lifetime and the PUBREC input path were inspected. A connected client that sends PUBREC for an unused packet ID creates an ACK-only entry that reaches the NULL pack after the retransmission delay.
